title: Letting Go
abstract: Abstract How are parents in America doing? Are they “helicopter parenting,” micromanaging the lives of their children? Failing to spend enough time with their children? While Americans raise questions about today’s parents, the challenges of parenting are not well understood. Based on numerous interviews with a diverse group of mothers of teenagers and young adults, Letting Go moves beyond popular views and offers a new understanding of parenting that demonstrates the challenging situations parents must navigate today as they guide their children through adolescence and young adulthood. Parents are expected to supervise the lives of their teens on an ongoing basis and ensure that they safely transition to young adulthood and on to adulthood and gain the credentials they need to succeed in an era when reaching adulthood has become more demanding. At the same time, parents must pull back and “let go” so their teens and young adults learn to take more responsibility for their lives. The negotiations with teens and young adults over control, trust, and letting go that mothers describe in this book offer an invaluable portrayal of the uncertainties and questions that underlie the day-to

title: Letting Go
abstract: Abstract Chapter 1 describes the need for more understanding of the challenges of parenting, which are underappreciated and often misunderstood, and it outlines the arguments of the book. It introduces the critical parental task of letting go and describes the tension parents face between maintaining control over key aspects of their teens’ lives so they remain safe and complete their education, while giving teens more freedoms and promoting their independence. Letting Go demonstrates that mothers are not simply in control of this process, that teens and young adults are active advocates for their views. Parenting and letting go take place through extended negotiations which sometimes go smoothly and sometimes involve conflict. Letting Go demonstrates the uncertainties parents face and the important role resources play in helping parents promote the success of their teens and young adults at a time when reaching adulthood has become a longer and more challenging process.

title: Becoming Adolescents and Pulling Away
abstract: Abstract Chapter 2 provides background on the changes mothers face in their relationships with their teens when they enter adolescence, and the challenges these changes present for the process of letting go. Mothers of all backgrounds describe their teens as “pulling away” during this time. Their teens begin to see things differently from their parents, they want to make more of their own decisions, and they challenge their parents’ authority. Mothers must negotiate with teens over their rights and privileges as teens demand to make more of their own decisions. Negotiations can go smoothly, and mothers and teens can experience conflicts. As teens enter young adulthood, parents face new decisions about how to support their young adults while promoting their autonomy and independence during a time when gaining the credentials to reach adulthood has become a more lengthy process. Young adults need financial support for a longer period than in the past.

title: Conclusion
abstract: Abstract Chapter 6 summarizes the argument of this book. Letting Go contributes to our understanding of parenting at two critical life stages, adolescence and young adulthood. And it expands knowledge of parenting more generally through mothers’ accounts of a key task of parenting: letting go, promoting the autonomy of teens and young adults. Parents are not simply in control of this process. Letting Go shows how parenting is a negotiated process between parents and their children, who are actively engaged in this process. This book also demonstrates the ways resources and social policy play a key role in parenting. The ability to promote the success of children, teens, and young adults is not only dependent on parents’ actions, but on the resources parents can access. Letting Go argues that there needs to be much greater social and governmental support for parenting.

title: Preface
abstract: Many years ago, I was the mother of two preschool-aged sons. My husband and I loved being parents. We were also very busy balancing our jobs and taking care of our children. We knew parenting would have its challenges. But what I didn’t realize until we actually had children was how much uncertainty was built into the job! There was no shortage of advice in the popular press: “Don’t use too much discipline or too little, monitor your children carefully, but don’t be over protective.” I was doing my best to raise children who would be safe and well-educated, and who would have an enjoyable childhood. But I wondered, Was I “helicopter parenting,” hovering too much? Or maybe I was too laid-back? Was I failing to understand the latest trends in parenting? I adored my sons, I was fascinated by all the new things they were doing, and they could be great fun to be with. At the same time, I found parenting very challenging; there were so many things to figure out and decisions to make. I often thought, “Why don’t more people write about what it’s really like to raise a child?” Bookstores are filled with books on parenting: “how-to” books, some by experts. But as one mother I interviewed fo

title: Promoting School Success and Preparing for Postsecondary Education
abstract: Abstract Chapter 4 explores the challenges mothers face in supporting their teens’ education. Mothers feel tremendous responsibility for ensuring that their teens succeed in school. They monitor teens’ progress in school, talk with their teens about assignments and deadlines, help them with school-related problems, attend parent-teacher meetings, and meet with teachers to learn of their teens’ progress in school. They provide encouragement for teens, help with their schoolwork as appropriate, and emotional support for teens who feel stress over their schoolwork. At the same time, mothers pull back and urge their teens to take responsibility for their schoolwork. Pulling back and letting go of some of their involvement in teens’ schoolwork can be challenging, as the stakes for successfully completing secondary school and obtaining some type of further education are high. Mothers feel they cannot let their teens fall behind. In the current era, the successful completion of high school and college is essential for achieving an adequate standard of living in adulthood.

title: Parenting Young Adults and Letting Go
abstract: Abstract Chapter 5 addresses the task of letting go as it takes shape in later adolescence and young adulthood. Young adults remain dependent on their parents for financial and other support as they attend college, enroll in training programs, or look for work. Many parents provide financial support as they are able during this time, some ask themselves how long they can or should support their young adults financially and in other ways, and at what point they should let go so that their young adults take on significant responsibility for their own lives. After they turn 21, some young adults are able to get jobs and start supporting themselves. Some may pursue postgraduate training. Some benefit substantially from financial support from parents and grandparents. Other young adults, however, particularly those who have not received more education or training after high school, may have difficulty finding a place in a competitive, uncertain economy.

title: Keeping Teens Safe at a Time of Risk
abstract: Abstract Chapter 3 examines the challenges mothers of adolescents face in keeping teens safe while letting go and allowing them more freedoms. Teens want to be out more and doing new things. They have increased access to information and activities, some of which parents consider risky. Mothers negotiate with their teens about where they can go and monitor their teens’ whereabouts as they go places on their own. As they work to keep teens safe, mothers debate with themselves about how to ensure the safety of their teens while not being too controlling or, as one mother said, how not to be “policing my teens all the time.” Mothers with resources are able to move to neighborhoods where they feel their teens will be safer. African American mothers face more challenges in keeping their teens and young adults safe given the possibility of police harassment and violence toward young African American men.

title: Civil Society Participation and Suicide Rates: A Cross-National Analysis
abstract: Previous valuable research has examined the effect individual-level social and psychological factors have on suicidality. However, scholarship has yet to investigate the role civil society participation plays in suicide rates cross-nationally. Thus, this study examines the effect civil society participation has on suicide rates in 156 countries from varying levels of development from 2000 – 2019 from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and North America. When including standard controls and controlling for potential endogeneity, the findings indicate that civil society participation, both political and non-political, has a negative and statistically significant effect on suicide rates. The results suggest that both political and non-political forms of civil society participation may produce positive social and psychological benefits that are associated with lower suicide rates.

title: The Dignity of Nonworking Men*
abstract: Abstract Studies have demonstrated the centrality of work and dignity in men's understanding of themselves and their place in society, especially in rural areas. However, previous studies of work and identity among men have generally drawn from the perspectives of the employed. From interviews with nonmetro prime‐age men (25–54 years old) who were out of the formal labor force ( N = 61), we find that men present themselves as deserving of dignified treatment. They do so by drawing on the values of work—describing themselves as skilled, hard workers with a strong sense of personal responsibility. Ironically, this sense of self‐worth can conflict with them remaining in the formal labor force because of how they are treated and how others conduct themselves on the job. In this rural setting, hegemonic market‐based values guide men even when outside the institution of work, yet some men find they can only resolve tension between these values and the realities of employment outside the formal labor market.

abstract: Corporate governance plays a key role in ensuring that companies act responsibly and legally in the pursuit of long-term, sustainable growth. Now in its fifth edition, Principles of Contemporary Corporate Governance offers a comprehensive introduction to the rules and regulations of corporate governance systems. It takes an inclusive stakeholder approach to examine how companies apply corporate governance principles in the private sector. The four-part structure has been consolidated and streamlined to provide logical coverage of fundamental contemporary themes and issues. The text has been updated to include new case studies and discussion of recent developments, such as the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic and the destruction of a sacred rock shelter at Juukan Gorge. A new section on corporate governance in Singapore offers insight into corporate governance internationally. Written by an expert author team, Principles of Contemporary Corporate Governance remains an indispensable resource for business and law students studying corporate governance.

title: Self-Worth Through Expertise: Experiences of Prime-Age Men Who are Out of the Formal Labor Force
abstract: Research on masculinity finds that men who are socioeconomically excluded or otherwise marginalized may create subcultures that eschew the values of mainstream society, such as by valuing and engaging in heavy drinking, fighting, bar culture, sports, and crime, as well as rejecting school success; recent discussions have also examined the rejection of expertise and experts as a related backlash to mainstream institutions. Using in-depth interview data, the present study examines how rural, prime-age men (n = 61) who are out of the labor force develop a sense of their own value without formal employment and the role expertise plays in them doing so. Most claim expertise and do so constructively, as they assert a positive sense of their own worth through their knowledge and skills (“I am a person who can … ”). Men make claims to the dignity of holding expertise while outside institutionalized employment roles. This suggests the portability of this cultural tool and that its use is not contingent on institutional endorsements. title: Prologue. Decoloniality as a Pedagogical Imperative in (Teacher) Education
The Economic Power of Capital and the Spread of COVID-19 in the United States: An Empirical Study
abstract: This study proposes a Marxian explanation to account for the spread of COVID-19 in the United States in 2020. Capital opposed and resisted public non-pharmaceutical interventions because they interfered with short-term profitability. The economy was prematurely reopened under the structural economic power of capital at the expense of society. This empirical analysis exploits the variation in the local economic power of capital across counties, measured by the county-level employment share of employees of private for-profit companies. If the structural economic power of capital in a county was more substantial, then the cumulative COVID-19 death rate and the unemployment rate were larger, and social distancing behaviors were discouraged in that county. Workplace safety was not guaranteed during the pandemic, potentially contributing to the spread of COVID-19. JEL Classification: B51, I18, P17

Development of Chronic Pain and High-Impact Chronic Pain across the U.S. Rural-Urban Continuum, 2019-2020
abstract: Abstract Purpose Rural health disadvantages are well-documented in previous literature, however research on rural-urban disparities in chronic pain outcomes is scarce. This paper fills this gap by examining pain prevalences and transitions across the rural-urban continuum (i.e., large central metro, large fringe metro, medium and small metro, and nonmetropolitan). Methods Based on the 2019-2020 National Health Interview Survey Longitudinal Cohort (NHIS-LC) data, we examined the disparities in pain prevalences and transitions among different pain states, including no pain, nonchronic pain, chronic pain and high-impact chronic pain (HICP), across the rural-urban continuum and by age, sex, race/ethnicity, and region. A test for linear trend was conducted to examine the significance of linear changes across the rural-urban continuum. Findings The findings reveal significant linear increases in the prevalence of chronic pain and HICP, as well as transitions from no pain to nonchronic pain and from nonchronic pain to more severe pain conditions, along the continuum from metropolitan to nonmetropolitan areas. title: MOUD 2.0: a clinical algorithm and implementation evaluation protocol for sublingual and injectable buprenorphine treatment of opioid use disorder
abstract: Background: Primary care is the initial contact point for most patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) but lacks tools for guiding treatment. Only a small fraction of patients access evidence-based care. Long-acting injectable buprenorphine has potential to improve medication adherence and program retention in low-barrier primary care treatment settings. We present the first clinical decision support algorithm incorporating long-acting buprenorphine (LAIB) in primary care. We include a protocol for a future evaluation of the algorithm's implementation process, "Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) 2.0," at a housing and integrated care clinic at a Federally Qualified Health Center. Methods: Literature review and expert consensus informed creation of the algorithm, which underwent iterative development with feedback from clinicians, staff, and patients. Patients are categorized by adherence to therapy and retention in the program, with recommendations for each category. Adherence is determined by urine screen supplemented by self-report. Preface
abstract: What Is It Like to Be an Addict? aims to do two things: first, to explain what substance addiction is, or better because substance addictions are a motley, to explain what substance addictions are, according to our best philosophy and science; second, to offer a humane and sensible ethics and politics of addiction. Addiction names a heterogeneous set of psychobiosocial behavioral disorders. Theorists who study the genetic, psychological, social, or neural features of addiction study an aspect of addiction. One cannot claim to know, from the perspective of any single discipline, what addiction is or what causes or comprises it. A proper theory of addiction will explain why psychological, social, genetic, and neural accounts are each in their own ways partial, and it will offer a method to integrate these partial accounts into a robust and ecumenical model. I offer such a method and model. One important feature of addiction is that it has an ineliminable subjective dimension. There is something existentially robust and existentially profound that it is like to be an addict from the addict’s point of view. The subjective aspects of addiction are not captured by the most exhaustive acc

title: Willing Addiction
abstract: Abstract We distinguish among willing addicts, unwilling addicts, and resigned addicts. Unwilling addicts want to undo their addiction but have not as yet found a way out. Resigned addicts wanted and tried to undo their addiction but have thrown in the towel. Willing addicts prefer, all things considered, to live their lives as addicts. Some question whether willing addicts exist. The chapter provides six examples, some of well-known people, who are willing addicts. This existence of willing addicts matters to the science and the ethics of addiction. Willing addicts are in whatever brain states addicts are allegedly in, but for them they do not judge that their addiction is bad. The existence of unwilling and resigned addicts, the large majority of addicts, call upon us to develop ethical, medical, and public policies that undo their terrible suffering.

title: The Addict’s Point of View
abstract: Abstract The chapter distinguishes the problem of addiction from four other related problems: widespread recreational use, the overdose epidemic, deaths of despair, and high mortality among the young. It argues for the necessity of the addict’s point of view for understanding and explaining addiction. We are introduced to the ten main themes of the book: Phenomenology (its importance); subjective and objective (tensions between how things seem to the addict and how things look to the behavioral and brain science that study addiction); addiction and identity; semantic issues; the disunity of addiction; failure of totalizing explanations; responsibility of addicts; willing, unwilling, and resigned addiction; shame for addiction; and the positive and negative ways Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous frame popular understanding of addiction.

title: What Is It Like to Be an Addict?
abstract: Abstract Addiction is best conceived as a psychobiological behavioral disorder. A common identifying feature of an addiction is that the addict (because of their relationship to a drug) undermines the aims they have for their own life. Sometimes they see this; sometimes they don’t. The common feature is, at first pass, existential, not neural, social, or psychological. The existential view is compatible with many social, psychological, and neural views, but they are not all compatible with the existential view. The chapter then explains how phenomenology—the study of how things seem from the subject’s point of view—can assist in understanding the appeals of different drugs to different people. The story of the author’s addiction as well as the testimony of other addicts supports the claim that the existential criterion of addiction is the tie that binds them, not any distinctive causal history or neural regularity.

title: Identity and Addiction
abstract: Abstract Many addictions originate in following lineage community practices that model approved substance-use norms and scripts. Cocktail hour; drinking at weddings and funerals; smoking pot before a concert; doing lines of coke at the dance club; and/or in the following practices of adolescent communities that try something new, different, or edgy—Ecstasy and Viagra, say. Many addicts come to identify with their addiction as part of a lifestyle, as a way of belonging to particular communities. The chapter discusses: 1. a variety of autobiographical and literary testimonies of addicts that reveal the ways addictions can be identity absorbing, how this grounds ambivalence about giving up an addiction; 2. arguments about whether we should think of the identity constituting aspects of many addictions as an essential aspect of the addiction, as a part of the reckoning involved in recovery.

title: Dedication
Hope and Addiction
abstract: Abstract The chapter assesses current theorizing about addiction, major debates in the field of addiction science, as well as various harm-reduction and treatment programs. Each of the three major theories of what addiction is—the self-medication model, the social dislocation model, and the brain disease model—have weaknesses. Each in its own way harms rather than helps motivate a holistic, integrated theory of addiction and sensible ethical and public policy. The chapter concludes with reasons for hope that integrated thinking about addiction will reduce addiction and substance misuse and help addicts and substance misusers heal.

title: The Shame of Addiction
abstract: Abstract This chapter addresses two main questions about the ethics of addiction: 1. What moral attitudes should addicts have toward themselves? Does it make sense for addicts to experience shame and guilt, to feel responsible for their addiction and what they do because they are addicts? 2. What moral attitudes should we have toward addicts? Do addicts deserve disappointment, disdain, anger, and resentment? The chapter criticizes glib views that say that addiction is a disease therefore moral categories do not apply, and argue that addicts themselves typically think they are responsible, and do so for good reason. It is explained how shame can be motivating for addicts and can help reveal that the addict sees their situation correctly. The chapter describes and defends a set of humane ethical attitudes we can have toward addicts, and that involve holding addicts to account, and treating them with compassion.

title: Note to Reader
abstract: Chapter 1, “The Addict’s Point of View,” Chapter 3, “Explaining Addiction,” and Chapter 8, “Hope and Addiction,” are entirely new. Chapter 2, “What Is It Like to Be an Addict?,” is substantially different from the 2007 published article with the same name. Chapter 6, “The Shame of Addiction,” has the same name and a similar theme as its 2013 ancestor, but almost entirely different content. Chapter 4, “Identity and Addiction,” Chapter 5, “Willing Addiction,” and Chapter 7, “The Phenomenal Authority of Alcoholics Anonymous” have close conceptual connections to their namesakes. But those three original essays have been diced, spliced, and rewritten in order to present an integrated theory of substance addiction. I have tried to make each chapter stand on its own; and I have tried to make every chapter accessible to lay readers and across disciplines. Taken together, they offer a view of what addiction is and how to understand and explain it, as well as some suggestions on how to prevent it and how to undo it. Chapter 3, “Explaining Addiction,” sketches the essentials of a naturalistic philosophy of mind, which I claim grounds the most plausible, defensible, and empirically well-suppor

title: Explaining Addiction
abstract: Abstract Understanding and explaining addiction require a credible view of the mind-body relationship, the relation of the conscious mind to unconscious mental processes and to an individual’s life history. The chapter offers such a theory, subjective realism. Subjective realism insists we are animals, material beings, but that there are two different modes of access to mind, one objective, one subjective. Subjective realism is metaphysically entirely naturalistic (no immaterial mental states), but epistemically dualist, which entails the necessity of the subjective point of view. Addiction is a psychobiosocial behavioral disorder that requires cooperation across the sciences, anthropology, sociology, psychology, and neuroscience, which we call the extended natural method. Many examples are provided.

title: The Phenomenal Authority of Alcoholics Anonymous
abstract: Abstract Alcoholics Anonymous speaks with authority and confidence about the nature, causes, and cure (such as there is one) of alcoholism and, in its progeny Narcotics Anonymous (NA), for other substance addictions, not just narcotic addiction. Two-thirds of treatment programs in North America are based on AA twelve-step principles. AA began not as a scientific or medical program. It began as an offshoot from an early twentieth-century Christian perfectionist movement. Many experts think that what AA and NA say about the nature of addicts and what ails them, and about what addiction is, is largely false, but that nonetheless AA and NA work. The chapter explores the extraordinary influence of AA and NA on the theory and treatment of addiction; whether what AA and NA say about addicts and addiction is true or not; and how AA could work even if they are false.

title: Community Opioid Use Recovery: Considering the Roles of Community Collaboration and Stigma
Estimating minimum wage effects on alcohol abuse and wages with alternative likely affected samples and models
venue: Review of Economics of the Household
abstract: Abstract We estimated effects of minimum wages on workers’ wages and alcohol abuse with samples defined by education and wages and using traditional two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) and new heterogeneous, Stacked, models that allow for staggered treatment timing. Alcohol abuse was measured with binary indicators of heavy and binge drinking and count data on days of binge drinking. Longitudinal data were drawn from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, 2005–2019. We investigated two samples of “likely affected” groups: the first—and most popular in the literature—was based on education i.e. people with at most a high school diploma; the second was based on wages, i.e. workers whose wages were ≤ 150% of minimum wages. Models included individual fixed effects. We found strong evidence that minimum wages lifted workers’ actual wages when “likely affected” was defined by wages but no evidence when “likely affected” was defined by education in both two-way-fixed-effects and Stacked models and across a variety of samples. We found most correlations between minimum wages and drinking were insignificant. While we found weak, suggestive evidence that minimum wages might reduce days of binge drinki

title: “The Dream Team”: Using a Health Equity and Social Justice Lens to Define the “T” in CIT
abstract: In the continuing wake of a historic reform movement that began in 2020, Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) programs are enjoying a moment in the national spotlight. Much of this attention is negatively focused on police officers and the departments in which they serve. However, police represent just one of a trio of stakeholders commonly associated with CIT, including community advocacy groups and mental health providers. The negative attention can be frustrating for police and other criminal justice professionals because they have no direct control over health care and how it is provided. Indeed, even the local governments that oversee most of the criminal justice activity associated with CIT have little direct control over health care infrastructure. However, local governments do directly control much of the infrastructure that influences underlying conditions of health such as access to clean water, sanitation, education, housing, and employment. Health equity and social justice frameworks make clear that multiple sectors need to collaborate and strategically plan a multi-pronged approach to addressing health equity, including mental health. title: Conclusion
abstract: Abstract The conclusion urges policymakers to carefully consider how a comprehensive set of interconnected protections can mitigate the impact of unpaid and precarious labour, thereby shaping a path toward inclusive and sustainable economic development. This approach is essential for ensuring the stability and security of society for all European citizens. The evidence presented in this book, and recalled in the conclusions, reveals that unpaid labour is not a peripheral issue but a fundamental aspect of the political economy of work in contemporary Europe. Too many workers in Europe find themselves in poorly designed or second-choice jobs, compelled to work unpaid hours, and struggling with insufficient paid work and limited opportunities for skill development. This situation has led to a highly segmented pattern of unpaid labour, with risks disproportionately affecting women, those with the least education, ethnic minorities, people with disabilities, and migrant workers.

title: Establishing a Theory of the Politics of Unpaid Labour
abstract: Abstract This chapter presents a novel theorization of the politics of unpaid labour. It looks at how the study of unpaid labour helps address inequality in precarious work, focusing on the class-based power structures of exploitation to explain how individuals experience the socio-economic activities surrounding work in their biographical histories in different ways. In essence, the theory behind the politics of unpaid labour advances our understanding of inequality in precarious work, explaining how the meanings attached to unpaid labour are embedded in different ways in individual income- and class-based features as well as employment structures and practices. These meanings also reflect the social norms underpinning stigma. The theory thus highlights the power dynamics generating the structural inequalities through which opportunities and resources to build resilience are circumscribed by class, including prestige, gender, and wealth.

title: Freelancing ‘for the Sake of Reputation’
abstract: Abstract The chapter empirically illustrates the politics of unpaid labour in the online platform sector in Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Italy, and Poland. Online platforms for freelancers vary, with different business models creating different conditions for freelancers. Dependent on a well-developed online reputation to secure a living income, many online freelancers sacrifice themselves and their family life for the sake of reputation. However, how an online reputation—and thus financial security—is built is greatly dependent on structures within and strategies of digital platforms, some of which foster precarity through their low rates, thus potentially exacerbating existing class differences characterized by the availability of resources to cope with the uncertainty of the work. This situation highlights how class-based circumstances intersect with platform structures, strategies, and dynamics, influencing the economic realities experienced by freelancers.

title: Methodology and Epistemology
Unpaid Labour, Labour Markets, and Capabilities
abstract: Abstract The chapter draws on the book’s notion of the politics of unpaid labour to examine the implications for the theory of capability in labour economics. Drawing from the novel theory presented in the book and supported by empirical findings in creative dance, residential care, and online freelancing, our argument asserts that the freedoms people enjoy—and which theories of ‘capability egalitarianism’ consider important for explaining equality in society—cannot be built ‘in silos’ as they are contingent upon a set of capability-providing collective arrangements of which labour market institutions and policies are key factors. In essence, labour market institutions and policies are just as important as civil, social, and political rights to guarantee equality in opportunities as they account for how far these rights are equally exercised.

title: Introduction
abstract: Abstract The Introduction presents the book’s main object and it unveils its main argument around the politics of unpaid labour. It brings out the principal themes (i.e., stigma and resilience) at the core of the book, it sheds light on the underpinning research questions, and it initiates its analytical contributions. In sum, the Introduction paves the way for the book’s central aim, that is to address inequality in precarious work for both waged (i.e., employees) and non-waged (i.e., self-employed workers) labour by an approach examining the politics of unpaid labour, delving into the dynamics and processes surrounding its occurrence and the extent to which individuals sustain it.

title: The Paid/Unpaid Labour Dichotomy
abstract: Abstract The chapter develops the critique stated in Chapter 1, discussing the implications of unpaid labour and precarious work for socially reproductive and gendered labour. It argues that precarious work is a complex and constantly evolving process requiring sophisticated analyses of the increasing reliance of workers and individuals on unpaid labour inside and outside the market. Unpaid labour inside the market accounts for new interdependencies as it requires resources—including socially reproductive (unpaid) labour outside the market—for it to be sustained as being how people build resilience. As access to such resources to build resilience is dependent on individual, household, and institutional circumstances, class-based inequality may arise, to the extent that certain occupations become out of reach for those less endowed with such resources.

title: Unpaid Labour and Inequality in Precarious Work
abstract: Abstract The chapter critically examines arguments of unpaid labour, precarious work, and inequality, all the while differentiating between employees in employment relationships and self-employed workers in service provision relationships. It initiates the exploration of the theoretical framework concerning the politics inherent to unpaid labour, discussing their potential to address the inequalities inherent to precarious work environments. This discussion strives to elucidate the rationale behind individuals’ experiences and the significance they ascribe to unpaid labour. It also works to embed the analysis of stigma and resilience into studies on unpaid labour, inequality, and precarious work. Stigma is the ‘social norm’ reflecting the social roles in place in a given setting, resilience is the availability and uptake of various resources.

title: Dance ‘for the Sake of Art’
abstract: Abstract The chapter empirically illustrates the politics of unpaid labour in dance (ballet) in Sweden and the Netherlands. Dance is a field that has suffered from sweeping austerity-driven funding cuts, especially in the Netherlands where it has become increasingly difficult to build up resilience against precarious work. These cuts have led to a decline in permanent employment and a rise in freelancing in the form of project work. Young people enter creative dance not for financial gain but for the sake of art. As much of the work is un- or underpaid, survival in dance relies heavily on having access to family resources, whether financial or social. Consequently, the sector has become class based, meaning that an individual’s social position and opportunities within this field are strongly influenced by their inherited socio-economic status, leading to the perpetuation of prestige and advantage through family connections and access to resources.

title: The Higher Education Wage Premium
abstract: Abstract Because higher education opens doors to more lucrative offers of employment, those who graduate from university tend to earn more than their counterparts who attain only a high school education. Notwithstanding variations across countries, this higher education wage premium has increased spectacularly over the past forty years. This chapter starts with an account of why we should worry about this trend—one that emphasizes the threat that it poses to equality of opportunity. The chapter then considers and evaluates two strategies for combatting the growing higher education wage premium, which relate to widening participation in higher education and to improving the economic prospects of those with no more than a high school education. This chapter argues in support of the latter, and elaborates on its implications for funding for vocational training.

title: Towards a Legal Right to Work from Home
abstract: Abstract Against the social and economic background of the recent pandemic and the rise of working from home to which it led, the aim of this chapter is to explore and answer the following two questions. First, are there compelling grounds for governments to promote opportunities for employees to work from home? And second, if so, how should labour market policymakers do this? The chapter’s conclusion is that there are weighty reasons for governments to increase the availability of opportunities to work from home, and, in particular, that they should do this by granting employees a legal right to work from home. What this means in policy terms, and how this departs from prevailing arrangements, are complex issues explored in further depth.

title: Gender Earnings Gaps
abstract: Abstract This chapter explores some normative questions relating to gender earnings gaps—that is, to the inequality in hourly and total earnings between men and women. In recent years, this gap has become a socially and politically urgent issue, provoking widespread condemnation. And while this topic is also being increasingly studied by empirically-minded social scientists, political philosophers have engaged with this scholarship to only a minimal degree. One aim of this chapter is to map out some of the relevant theoretical terrain, emphasizing the moral importance of the fact that much of the disparity in earnings between men and women emerges from the fact that young parents have strong incentives to specialize as breadwinners and caregivers. Much of the work in this chapter is exploratory, reflecting the nascent state of the philosophical literature.

title: Occupational Harms (and Benefits)
abstract: Abstract The aim of the previous chapter was to outline the empowerment model and to describe some of its central attractions. The aim of this chapter is to strengthen my defence of the empowerment model by contrasting it with its most serious competition, namely the occupational harms model. Proponents of this view claim that the goal of labour market policymaking should be to protect individuals against various unavoidable occupational harms—that is, against particular harms that they suffer because of their need to participate in labour markets. Accordingly, when diagnosing injustices in labour markets, those drawn to this approach focus directly on specified harms that workers endure as a result of having to sell their labour. Though there is much to recommend in this view, this chapter argues that the occupational harms model offers less practical guidance than the empowerment model, and is less theoretically attractive for this reason.

title: Conclusion
abstract: Abstract This brief chapter highlights some of the themes of the book, especially those relating to automation, artificial intelligence, and the future of work. It cautions against sensationalist narratives relating to these issues, and instead emphasizes the need for empirically informed philosophical reflection to guide the political decisions that shape the labour market. It contends that technology is a double-edged sword that brings both threats and opportunities, affecting individuals’ lives in myriad ways. It concludes with some advice for governments, who must be prepared to make courageous choices to protect workers’ interests and who cannot leave these matters to the force of the market alone.

title: Work Hours and Free Time
abstract: Abstract The aim of this chapter is to contribute to defences of working time policies and, in particular, to offer some remarks in support of the justifiability of the four-day work week. The chapter distinguishes different kinds of argument that may be voiced by those sympathetic to this conclusion, and considers several objections, including from those who condemn shorter work hours on the alleged grounds that this will likely reduce economic output. In doing so, the analysis sheds new light on the appeal of the stationary state. The chapter concludes with some discussion of what is most attractive with the four-day work week in comparison with other policies that improve access to free time.

title: The Significance of Employment
abstract: Abstract The aim of this chapter is to shed light on various disputes about the significance of employment, and then, using the empowerment model, to draw out some of the implications of these commitments for labour market policymaking, particularly in a world of artificial intelligence. The analysis starts with an account of the value of employment, which serves as a foundation on which to defend policies whose purpose is to eliminate involuntary unemployment. It then defends this line of reasoning against critics who contend that this view fetishizes work. The chapter includes a more technical discussion of whether it’s wrong for governments to promote employment since doing so unfairly penalizes those who’ve no desire to be employed, and concludes with a discussion of the appeal of basic income.

title: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This chapter clarifies the main aims of this book, which are to develop and defend a novel way of theorizing about the demands of justice in the labour market, called the empowerment model, and then to draw on this model to shed light on a range of ongoing disputes about the future of work. The chapter also introduces some of the book’s main themes, particularly relating to social class, the demands of liberalism, and the relevance of empirical scholarship to political philosophy. It then summarizes the text’s structure, including the division of labour between Parts I and II, before concluding with some brief remarks about method.

title: The Empowerment Model
abstract: Abstract This chapter proposes a novel way of theorizing about the demands of justice in the labour market that is capable of shedding light on various economic trends and the injustices with which they are associated. Its aim is to explicate and defend the deceptively simple sounding claim that, within limits, the goal of labour market policymakers should be to secure individuals’ equal bargaining power or, when this is unwise, to protect them against the disadvantages to which their lack of equal bargaining power might otherwise give rise. I call this the empowerment model. The chapter highlights and defends one especially controversial component of this commitment, namely is ambition-sensitivity.

title: Beyond Bargaining Power
abstract: Abstract This chapter evaluates three closely related objections to the empowerment model, each of which targets the fact that, even if governments were to secure individuals’ equal bargaining power, many workers may still be forced to sell their labour to others to make ends meet. The first of these focuses on the illegitimacy of most workplace authority; the second targets the involuntary nature of many employment contracts; and the third emphasizes the subordination that many workers endure. Though each offers valuable insights, the chapter concludes that none of these lines of reasoning justifies abandoning or substantially revising the empowerment model. The chapter ends with some remarks about the appeal and limitations of workplace democracy.

title: South American aging populations: Challenges and opportunities for addressing mental health issues
abstract: Abstract This chapter focuses on aging and mental health in South America with an emphasis on cultural factors and social determinants of health relevant to dementia and other mental disorders in older adults. Four countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Colombia) are highlighted, together with South American immigrants to the United States. Historical and demographic information, cultural factors, the impact of the aging process on mental and neurological disorders and type of healthcare systems available to address these problems are included under each country. Specific issues relevant to South American aging populations including special populations, environmental and climate issues, dementia, substance use, task shifting strategies as key interventions, and potential resources to expand services and research focusing on mental health issues of older adults are highlighted.

title: Applications to Work as Paid Employment
Introduction: Actions, Intentions, and Institutions
Right-Wing Populism: Morbid Symptoms of Global Capitalism
venue: Perspectives on Global Development and Technology
abstract: Abstract With the ascent of Donald Trump and other authoritarian leaders it is vitally important to understand why middle-class and working-class voters are attracted to authoritarian solutions. Neoliberalism and globalization have provided the basis for alienation from the political process and democratic institutions. But to understand the psychological and cultural reasons we can turn to Erich Fromm, Herbert Marcuse, and others from the Frankfort school to explain how fear, shame, and despair feed the far-right.

title: Predatory rentierism in irregular migration: how debts, threats, and rackets shape lives on the move
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
abstract: This article introduces the framework of predatory rentierism to account for pervasive but under-theorized forms of violence and their perpetrators across the process of irregular migration. Predatory rentierism is the practice of deriving gains from the ownership or control of scarce assets in a manner that threatens the renter's basic rights, and it can take various forms, from extortion and bribery to usurious loans and ransoms. Drawing on ethnographic observation and 70 semi-structured and in-depth interviews in Guatemala and the U.S., I demonstrate how predatory rentierism interpenetrates each node in the migration trajectory, thriving on the intersecting marginalities of irregular migrants. I argue that the predatory rentierism framework helps to surface under-examined drivers of migration, make sense of transit and integration experiences, and contribute to understanding why remittances can fail to produce sustainable hometown development. I close by outlining future directions for studying predatory rentierism in irregular migration.

abstract: Addiction is a highly prevalent brain disease. It is a major cause of many secondary forms of medical illness and accidents, and it is a leading root cause of death. The disease attacks the circuits of the brain that govern motivational learning and control. It is defined by increasingly compulsive drug seeking and use, despite the accumulation of negative medical, social, and psychiatric consequences. Because the disease also impacts brain systems governing the exercise of free-will, decision-making, and insight, it is often judged, criminalized, and stigmatized, which are countertherapeutic social responses to the disease. Addiction psychiatry is a field of psychiatry that is uniquely trained to treat the entire spectrum of addictions and mental illness, especially for mainstream dual-diagnosis patients who suffer with combinations of these disorders. The epidemiology of addiction shows that the disease is not evenly distributed in the population. Rather, it tends to concentrate in people with genetic, developmental, and environmental risk factors, many of which overlap with those that also produce mental illness. title: Preface
abstract: This book makes the case for neoliberalism as a useful lens for understanding a broad range of political phenomena, those pertaining to the political order and the governing of advanced Western societies, but also others that signal rupture and conflict at the extreme right and left ends of the political spectrum, often referred to as identity politics. I arrive at this topic through a long-standing interest in immigration and citizenship policies and surrounding ethnic and multiculturalism struggles, which I had initially looked at from the vantage point of advancing liberalism.i However, neoliberalism does not equal liberalism. To clearly demarcate and set the two apart, head-on,ii and without denying their common roots and shared features, is the main purpose of this book. The notion of neoliberalism is rejected by many as shrill and overspent. A proper use of it needs to avoid both: a narrow understanding as a political economy category, but also an overly broad understanding as an “encompassing constructivist framework,” as Patrick Le Galès (2016, 154) criticized a line of thinking pioneered by French philosopher Michel Foucault, in which everything from states to subjectiviti

title: End of Neoliberalism?
abstract: Abstract This concluding chapter turns to the biggest crisis of world society since World War II and asks what role neoliberalism has played in it. Some have argued that the COVID-19 pandemic management’s priority to the protection of life, and the proactive role of the state in it, have ushered in the end of political neoliberalism. This chapter argues against this that authoritarianism, the original political form of neoliberalism, has had a remarkable revival in states’ public health management, consisting of a double strategy of lockdown and quasi-mandatory mass vaccination. Furthermore, among the long-term effects of the pandemic is the accelerated digitalization of social life, which has strengthened the Big Firm–Big State alliance that has marked real-existing neoliberalism from the beginning. Considering the authoritarian pandemic management and control-minded digitalization, one must conclude that freedom is the scarce good of the future, ironically the good that neoliberalism had originally set out to recover.

title: End of the Liberal-Democratic Synthesis
abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses six political forms of neoliberalism, from the point of view of order. First, neoliberalism’s oldest and recurrent political form is authoritarianism, which most clearly expresses neoliberalism’s constitutive unease with democracy. Secondly, and diametrically opposed to it, there is governance as neoliberalism’s newest and most closely associated form today, which is meant to bring back a modicum of democracy, deceptively as shall be argued. A third political form, technocracy, provides much of the content and guiding principles of governance, which likes to fashion itself as rational problem-solving, while eschewing the right–left distinction. The fourth and fifth political forms of neoliberalism, federation and constitutionalism, are exemplarily combined in the European Union, which this chapter highlights as a model case of a neoliberal polity. Finally, there is meritocracy, which is less a form of rule than the central legitimizing formula of the competitive society that political neoliberalism seeks to build.

title: Epigraph
abstract: “The fact that the ‘free world’ had an alternative made it an alternative itself . . . (W)hen freedom is the only reality, you are no longer free.”

title: The Identity Left
abstract: Abstract Under political neoliberalism, much of the left has shifted from class to identity politics, with a focus on race and gender. Unlike the populist right, whose main foothold is the electoral process, the identity left has found a strong foothold in public institutions, the media, and the corporate world. Its legal-moral foundations are civil rights and antidiscrimination laws and principles, which have outlawed formal racism and sexism since the 1960s. As a result, smaller injuries, of the immaterial and symbolic kind, take on bigger proportions, amplified by the fact that the speech-dependent and increasingly speech-regulating academy is one of the major platforms of the identity left. This chapter compares and contrasts antiracism and transgender as prominent instances of left identity politics today. Both present themselves as forces of rupture and radical change, but both are deeply formatted by neoliberal precepts: “race parity” on the part of antiracism, and “hyper-individualism” on the part of transgender.

title: The Populist Right
abstract: Abstract This chapter argues that right-wing populism, while often taken to be the main opposite force to political neoliberalism, advances “illiberal democracy,” which is not a solution to democracy’s problems but an aggravation of them. Populism’s objective root cause is massively increased inequality and insecurity because of neoliberalism, and the concomitant decline of the vision and reality of middle-class society. However, not these economic woes but cultural change, particularly that brought by immigration, has set the agenda of the populist right. Because the latter is also nationalist, the question arises as to what kind of nationalism it is and how it expresses itself in policy terms. With a focus on Europe, it is argued that, in the West, populist nationalism has expressed itself, for instance, in welfare chauvinism, although with limited impact. In Eastern Europe, by contrast, populist nationalism has fueled the rise of an “illiberal state,” as the case of Viktor Orbán`s Hungary demonstrates.

title: From Right to Left, and Back?
abstract: Abstract This chapter traces the evolution of political neoliberalism, which matured from right-wing movement into political order, consented by the left also. The first part lays out the ideological contours of the Third Way, which repositioned the left in an unambiguously pro-capitalist direction after the fall of Communism. The second part shows the policy import of Third Way thinking in a new conception of the welfare state, as social investment. Thirdly, the right-to-left turn of neoliberalism has also expressed itself in a thin multiculturalism surrounding diversity and antidiscrimination, both particularly strong in (but not exclusive to) the United States. Finally, some have argued, with special attention to the European Union, that after the 2008 Financial Crisis neoliberalism has recovered its original authoritarian and democracy-thumping face. Against this, it is argued that authoritarianism is less a distinct third phase than ever-present possibility or even aspect of a neoliberal order.

title: Liberalism versus Neoliberalism
abstract: Abstract This chapter seeks to distinguish neoliberalism from liberalism, both understood more as political than as philosophical doctrines. Neoliberalism shares with classical liberalism a commitment to toleration (today eulogized as “diversity”), freedom, individualism, and the rule of law, which is the same for all. However, as an in-depth analysis of the work of Friedrich Hayek—one of neoliberalism’s chief theorists—shows, neoliberalism parts ways with liberalism in several respects: in absolutizing freedom over all other values, in a thin and formalistic understanding of equality that repudiates social justice, and in a general hostility to democracy, with which liberalism had been in a tension-fraught but stable synthesis. Crucially, whereas liberalism respects the autonomy of spheres in a functionally differentiated society, neoliberalism is “market fundamentalism” that shows no such respect.

title: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This introduction illustrates the central task of the book: to distinguish clearly between neoliberalism and liberalism, along different understandings of “citizenship,” neoliberal versus liberal. Even astute scholars and critics of neoliberalism do not always meet this test. The introduction further distinguishes between two different understandings of neoliberalism, a narrow understanding as a political economy category and a broad understanding as a sector- and policy-transcending political rationale. While the risks of a broad understanding are conceded, this book`s preference for a broad understanding is defended. The rest of the introduction provides a brief overview of the main themes and chapters of the book.

abstract: Abstract We have argued in this volume that democratic backsliding involves the slow erosion of institutions, processes, and norms. To explain backsliding, political historians, economists, sociologists, and political scientists (who we have referred to collectively as institutionalists) have focused on the role of elites, economic and social disparities, and civil society organizations. While insightful, the institutionalist literature has had little to say about the role of social media and other digital platforms. On the other hand, offering what we have called the technocentric understanding of backsliding, scholars focusing on social media have little to say about social and economic power structures and the erosion of democratic institutions. In chapter one, Bennett and Livingston present an integrated framework that explains how digitally networked publics interact with more traditional party organizations and electoral processes to bring once-scattered extremist factions into conservative parties. In this concluding chapter, we consider possible reasons why so much scholarly attention has been paid to the technocentric explanation of democratic backsliding. We suggest that

abstract: Abstract Epistemic democrats indirectly evaluate democratic decisions by directly evaluating the inputs into the election. However, the fundamental problem of measurement in the philosophy of science shows that procedures are often as difficult to evaluate as outcomes. This paper brings this highly refined framework into political philosophy to show that epistemic democrats face an analogous ‘fundamental problem of evaluation’. This cross-fertilization of political philosophy with the philosophy of science shows that the quality of democratic mechanisms and their inputs regarding their ability to track the truths of justice is as difficult to evaluate as the quality of the resulting decisions themselves.

Can alcohol use explain the increase in educational inequalities in all‐cause mortality after 2010 in the USA? A three‐way interaction analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: In the United States, the educational gap in all-cause mortality and life expectancy has dramatically increased since 2010. This study investigated whether alcohol use has contributed to the increasing educational gap in mortality by testing the three-way interaction of alcohol use, education and period on all-cause mortality. DESIGN: Cohort study with 9 years' follow-up on average. SETTING: United States. PARTICIPANTS: 207 223 males and 255 833 females aged 25 years and older from the 2000-2018 National Health Interview Survey. MEASUREMENTS: The outcome was time to all-cause death or last presumed alive by 12/31/2019 based on the National Death Index. Three-way interaction effects between educational attainment (bachelor degree or more vs. high school degree or less), alcohol use (drinking >60 g/day in males and >40 g/day in females vs. lifetime abstinence) and period (after vs. before 2010) were investigated on the multiplicative and additive scales using Cox proportional hazards and Aalen's additive hazards models, respectively, with age as the time scale. Introduction
abstract: This brief introduction argues that the current, swirling debates over the ills of social media are largely a reflection of larger forces in our society. Social media is accused of creating political polarization, yet polarization long predates social media and pervades every aspect of our society. Social media is accused of a liberal bias and “wokeness”; but in fact, conservative commentators accuse every major institution of our society, including academia, the press, and corporate America, of the same sin. Social media is said to be causing psychological harm to young people, especially young women. But our society’s tendency to impose image-consciousness on girls and young women, and to sexualize girls at ever younger ages, pervades not just social but also mainstream media, the clothing industry, and our culture more generally. And as with polarization, this phenomenon long predates the advent of social media. In short, the supposed ills of social media are in fact the ills of our broader culture. It is just that the pervasiveness of social media makes it the primary mirror in which we see ourselves; and apparently, we do not much like what we see.

title: Trade and Environment
abstract: Chapter 12 examines international environmental issues as they intersect with trade issues. We analyze the case law produced by the World Trade Organization (WTO) in various disputes in which the prerogative of free trade stumbled over the regulatory measures that states have enacted to protect endangered species and human health. Some of the cases that have made headlines include national measures to protect the dolphins when fishing for tuna; restricting the use of growth hormones in cattle; and the regulation of GM products. This chapter demonstrates how international environmental law has had a lasting impact on trade law and how it has helped refashion the notion of free trade.

title: Preface and Acknowledgments
abstract: The name of the degree emblazoned on my diploma from my undergraduate studies reads “Bachelor of Medical Sciences, Honors Specialization in Physiology.” Having mostly taken courses in the “basic medical sciences” during the program, I graduated with the impression that the science of medicine was laboratory science and that clinical medicine was something like applied physiology. Introductory books on the history of medicine often reinforced this idea, sometimes identifying the rise of “modern medicine” in the nineteenth or twentieth century with transformative discoveries in laboratory research or with “laboratory medicine” or “biomedicine.” In medical school, there were times when this afterimage was further burned into my retinas, especially during preclinical training in the classroom and the dissecting room, when I rehashed much of what I’d previously learned. But I came to see that this picture was at best incomplete and left out the impressive role of epidemiological sciences in molding our understanding of disease and evidence, our medical concepts, and our medical reasoning. It was the philosophy of medicine that first clued me in to the missing story of epidemiology in mo

title: The New Medical Model
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines what made medicine modern in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and in what ways medicine today is a new modern medicine. It rejects the views that effective medicine made medicine modern and that contemporary medicine is laboratory medicine or biomedicine. It argues instead that modern medicine is modern scientific medicine, clinical medicine integrated with and modeled after modern research sciences. While laboratory science–based medicine was the medical model a century ago, the new medical model since the Second World War is an epidemiological medicine resulting from a threefold epidemiologic transition in disease, evidence, and science. In epidemiological medicine, clinical medicine is integrated with the new sciences of epidemiology.

title: Medical Interventions and Risk
abstract: Abstract This chapter explores the meaning of medical risk in two parts. In the first part, it examines what it means to be a preventive or curative medical intervention, arguing that such interventions reduce the risk of a medical condition in a population compared to their omission, commonly by disrupting a mechanism for the condition, but with varying individual-level effects. In the second part, it examines interpretations of patient-level probabilities inferred from population-level risks and argues that rather than patient-level risks or propensities, medicine ought to interpret these probabilities as rational degrees of belief that quantify epidemiological uncertainty, or uncertainty about the distribution of patient outcomes in the population and where in the distribution a particular patient falls.

title: Medical Evidence and Prediction
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the epistemology of evidence-based medicine (EBM). EBM descends from an empiric tradition of predicting directly from experience with previous patients. The chapter names EBM’s standard model of prediction in which inferences are made from the results of epidemiological studies the “Risk Generalization-Particularization Model”. It names EBM’s implicit view of medical evidence in which evidence consists of measurements of clinical outcomes (especially risks) the “measurement theory”. After unearthing the assumptions upon which the standard model of prediction relies, the chapter defends an alternative “argument theory of medical evidence”, in which evidence is facts or data that support premises in arguments for medical hypotheses.

title: The Nature of Chronic Diseases and Mental Disorders
abstract: Abstract This chapter revolves around a search for a metaphysical theory that might provide a general understanding of the nature of chronic diseases and mental disorders, particularly their chronicity and the fact that they are frequently asymptomatic (the silent disorder phenomenon). It defends a dispositional theory of chronic diseases and mental disorders according to which they are bodily dispositions toward clinical findings. The dispositional theory suggests that difficulties in explaining, predicting, and intervening in chronic diseases and mental disorders might be due to their lacking specific pathology or a particular causal base common to each case of a disease.

title: Therapeutic Skepticism
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines varieties of therapeutic skepticism that are motivated by the ubiquity of biased medical evidence. It argues that medical evidence is biased or misleading when it supports a premise in an unsound medical argument. The chapter considers several objections to Medical Nihilism, a skepticism requiring us to have low confidence in the effectiveness of medical interventions. It then defends Medical Meta-Evidentialism, which asks us to become more skeptical of therapeutic study results and therapeutic effectiveness due to biased evidence without necessarily having low confidence. Meta-Evidentialism is supported by meta-research findings that serve as evidence of research bias and are an underappreciated source of evidence for therapeutic evaluation.

title: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This chapter introduces the project in which The New Modern Medicine is engaged: a philosophical examination of the new modern medicine and its new medical model, epidemiological medicine. The chapter provides a glimpse into elements of the new modern medicine by comparing diabetes today to diabetes a century ago. It introduces seven problems of the new modern medicine to motivate the project: molecular reductionism; multifactorial etiology; chronicity, asymptomaticity, and variable pathology; evidence hierarchies; meaning of medical risk; external validity of clinical trials; and biased evidence. It situates the present work in the field of philosophy of medicine. Last, it provides a synopsis of the book’s subsequent chapters.

title: Causation and Classification of Disease
abstract: Abstract This chapter investigates the contemporary causation and classification of disease. It seeks to understand why many infectious diseases have a specific universal etiology while noncommunicable diseases have a multifactorial etiology. Some have proposed a monocausal model in which infectious diseases are classified according to a specific cause, yielding theoretical and practical benefits. However, the monocausal model is a myth. Rather, a constitutive model is used to classify all diseases, a model in which the disease is classified according to the bodily condition of which it consists. The constitutive model can help establish universal etiology by defining diseases according to a specific pathology. Rather than specific etiology, specific pathology was the key conceptual revolution of modern medicine and can help medicine explain and combat disease.

title: Twenty-First-Century Medicine
abstract: Abstract This chapter considers competing visions for twenty-first-century medicine: epidemiological medicine, radical personalized medicine, and postmodern medicine. In epidemiological medicine, scientific medicine is based in the science of epidemiology. In radical personalized medicine, it is instead grounded in laboratory molecular biology. In postmodern medicine, scientific medicine loses its privileged authority. It is argued that epidemiological medicine is the most realistic near-term possibility. Yet epidemiological medicine could increasingly integrate molecular epidemiology according to a precision medicine model. Meanwhile, the resilience of pseudosciences like homeopathy and resistance to scientific medicine like that seen during the COVID-19 pandemic should force serious reflection on the problems and limits of epidemiological medicine, which for better and for worse has been the dominant model of scientific medicine for decades.

title: Theories of Contagion and Cancer
abstract: Abstract This chapter investigates theories of disease in modern medicine in search of a theory of cancer. Using the germ theory of contagious diseases as a prototype, it argues that a theory of disease unifies models of the pathogenesis of diseases within a family of disease. Somatic mutation theory, a theory of cancer, developed out of epidemiology and molecular biology toward the end of the 1900s and views cancers as diseases of uncontrolled cell proliferation, genetic alteration, and molecular dysregulation. The chapter considers whether scientific frameworks better characterize medical research than scientific theories and whether somatic mutation theory promotes a problematic molecular reductionism.

title: Effect Measures and the Sufficient-Component Cause Model
abstract: According to the sufficient-component cause (SCC) model, medical interventions are component causes within sufficient causes of health outcomes (Rothman 1976). For any preventive or curative medical intervention, we can divide the sufficient causes of a health outcome Y into four types: A: MT=1, CD=0 B: MT=1, X=0 C: MNT=1 D: CH=1, X=1 A, B, C, and D are types of sufficient cause, while MT, CD, MNT, CH, and X are types of component cause. Each sufficient cause is present for an individual when and only when all of its listed conditions are met. Each sufficient cause and each component cause can be represented by a dichotomous variable (0,1), where 1 represents individual-level “exposure” and 0 represents individual-level “non-exposure.” X is a preventive or curative medical intervention, while Y is the health outcome it cures or prevents. MT and MNT are mechanisms or pathology that cause Y. MT represents mechanisms targeted by X, while MNT represents mechanisms not targeted by X. CD represents “disruption cofactors” that help X to disrupt MT and cure/prevent Y. CH represents “harm cofactors” that help X cause Y, a paradoxical harm. Exposure to MT or MNT occurs given at least one com

title: Problems of Extrapolation
abstract: Abstract This chapter dissects the problem of extrapolating from clinical trials into two components: a logical problem of extrapolation and an evidential problem of extrapolation. The logical problem requires extrapolators to construct a good extrapolation argument, while the evidential problem requires extrapolators to determine what kind of evidence would support that argument. Both problems must overcome a daunting challenge known as the extrapolator’s circle. The chapter examines existing solutions to the problems of extrapolation before proposing a new solution to the logical problem called mechanism-cofactor analysis and a new solution to the evidential problem relying on structural analogies.

title: Contesting the new right’s global war on education: toward an antifascist metapolitics
abstract: This article analyzes the emergence of the global New Right and its assault on democratic education. Drawing on Frankfurt school critical theory and international studies of the far-right, the authors examine the structural, psychological, and educational preconditions that have enabled a far-right authoritarian wave across national contexts including the United States, Brazil, Hungary, Italy, and India. They argue that the New Right has taken advantage of the conjunctural crises of global capitalism and neoliberalism through ‘metapolitical’ strategies including appropriation of progressive-left concepts such as Gramscian cultural hegemony and decolonisation. Central to this effort is a global authoritarian assault on education and cultural institutions, aimed at dismantling critical literacy, academic freedom, and democratic subject formation. The article proposes an ‘antifascist metapolitics’ for educational studies that resists the instrumentalization of education under both neoliberalism and neofascism, and calls for pedagogical and political strategies that cultivate historical consciousness, pluralism, and democratic solidarity. The authors conclude by advocating for internat

title: Socioeconomic Status and Health
venue: The Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Health, Illness, Behavior, and Society
abstract: Abstract Socioeconomic status (SES), a measure of income, education, and prestige, is inextricably linked to health, with higher levels of SES typically associated with healthier lifestyles, lower incidence of disease, lower mortality rates, and overall better physical and mental health. There has been long‐standing interest in the effect of social inequalities on health, with attention being paid to both the possible mechanisms driving the SES–health relationship and the most salient indicators of SES for disease outcomes. This article explores the measurement of SES and health, the mechanisms linking SES to health outcomes, and potential interventions. A better understanding of the SES–health relationship offers opportunities to improve population health and to achieve health equity.

Envisioning the Future of Work: From Ideas to Reforms
abstract: ABSTRACT Two different theoretical perspectives concerning technology and the future of work are examined. One is linked to mainstream economics, whereas the other is associated with critical (‘post‐work’) discourse. Ideas about work—its nature and impacts on well‐being—matter in both perspectives. Indeed, they shape visions of a ‘better’ or ‘ideal’ future. They also influence policy responses to new technology. A critique is presented of the ways that work and its possible futures are understood. This critique is used to develop a different set of ideas about how technology might be harnessed to reduce the burden and raise the quality of work. The ability of ideas to effect reforms in and of work—ideas that have currency now and possible radical alternatives—is also assessed.
